blurb: Models that think before they answer: why thinking longer helps, the tricks for spending that effort, and how we test it.

steps.p: A reasoning model writes a long private chain of thought — trying ideas, checking, backtracking — before giving its final answer.
Unlike prompting "think step by step", these models were trained with reinforcement learning to reason well, rewarded when their final answers were right.
Before, you made AI smarter mainly by training bigger models. OpenAI's o1 (2024) showed a second dial: let the model think longer at answer time.

steps.h: More thinking, more right — up to a point
steps.p: On maths and coding, accuracy climbs as the model is allowed more thinking tokens. On simple questions, extra thinking mostly adds cost.
steps.analogy: More time helps on a hard exam question, not on "What's 2 + 2?"

steps.p: Thinking tokens cost money and time, even when they're hidden from you. Some apps let you set a thinking budget.

cards.q: What new way to make AI smarter did OpenAI's o1 highlight?
options: Spending more computing at answer time, by thinking longer
cards.why: Thinking longer. Instead of only making models bigger, you can let the same model spend more effort on each question. This is called test-time compute.

cards.statement: Reasoning models beat standard models on every kind of task.
cards.why: False. They shine at maths, code and logic. For quick facts, casual chat or simple writing, they're slower and costlier with little gain.

cards.statement: With some services, you pay for a reasoning model's hidden thinking even though you never see it.
cards.why: True. Thinking tokens are generated like any others and billed as output. A short answer can hide thousands of thinking tokens.

cards.title: OpenAI's o3 scored 75.7% on the ARC-AGI puzzle test at modest cost in December 2024 — and 87.5% with far more computing.
cards.detail: ARC had resisted AI for years; earlier models scored far lower. The high-effort run cost much more per puzzle than paying a human to solve it.

options: The most tokens the model may spend reasoning before it answers
How much you pay per month
cards.why: The cap on thinking. A small budget is quick and cheap; a large one helps on hard problems.

steps.p: Write a longer chain of thought, checking and revising along the way.
Produce several independent answers and pick one — by majority vote, or by having a checker score each.
Many of these tricks work because checking an answer is often much easier than finding it.
steps.analogy: Solving a sudoku is hard; checking a finished one takes seconds.

steps.p: Explore a tree of partial solutions, dropping branches that look bad and continuing the promising ones — like a chess player thinking moves ahead.
Easy questions need little effort; hard ones need more. Matching effort to difficulty gets the most out of each dollar.

options: Generating N answers and keeping the one the checker scores highest
cards.hint: Look at the flow in step 2.
cards.why: Many tries, best one kept. If any of the N attempts is good and the checker can recognise it, you get it.

cards.q: Why do so many of these methods rely on checking?
options: Checking a solution is often much easier than producing one
cards.why: Verifying is easier. Running tests on code or plugging a number back into an equation is cheap and reliable, so lots of attempts plus a good check beats one careful attempt.

cards.statement: Majority voting helps open-ended essays as much as it helps maths problems.
cards.why: False. Voting needs answers that can match exactly, like "42". Every essay is different, so there's nothing to count.

cards.title: Spending answer-time effort wisely let a small model beat one 14 times larger on some problems.
cards.detail: A 2024 Google DeepMind study (Snell et al.) found that giving harder problems more thinking could outperform a much bigger model that didn't think longer.

options: The chance that at least one of 10 attempts is correct
cards.why: At least one in ten right. It shows what's possible if you can recognise the right attempt — useful when you have a checker, like tests for code.

steps.p: A benchmark is a fixed exam. Once top models score near 100%, it can no longer tell them apart — it's "saturated".

visual.caption: Illustration of a benchmark filling up over a few years.

steps.p: GSM8K, about 8,500 grade-school word problems, was hard in 2021. Top models now get almost all of it right.
Competition maths (AIME), research-level maths (FrontierMath) and expert questions from many fields (Humanity's Last Exam) took over.
ARC-AGI uses coloured-grid puzzles that need no special knowledge but are new each time — testing whether a model can adapt, not recall.
steps.analogy: The difference between a quiz on facts you studied and a brain-teaser you've never seen.

steps.p: If test questions appear online, they can end up in training data, inflating scores. Fresh, private tests guard against this.

cards.q: AIME, often used to test reasoning models, is…
options: A US high-school maths competition with 15 problems and whole-number answers from 0 to 999
cards.why: A tough maths contest. Answers are whole numbers, so marking is automatic — handy for both testing and training.

cards.statement: GSM8K (grade-school maths word problems) is still a hard test for the best models.
cards.hint: Look at what happened to school maths in step 2.
cards.why: False. Top models now score well above 90%. It's saturated, so it says little about the frontier.

cards.q: When FrontierMath launched in late 2024, the best models solved roughly what share of its problems?
cards.why: Under 2%. The problems were written by research mathematicians. Within months reasoning models were scoring far higher — another treadmill turn.

cards.title: Humanity's Last Exam contains about 2,500 expert-written questions across dozens of subjects.
cards.detail: Released in early 2025 by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI, it was built from questions that stumped leading models. Initial top scores were under 10%.

cards.statement: ARC-AGI puzzles require lots of specialised expert knowledge.
cards.why: False. Most people can solve them with no special training. They test spotting a new pattern from a few examples — something AI found surprisingly hard.

steps.p: Models sometimes spend thousands of tokens on a simple question, second-guessing a correct answer into a wrong one.
Trained to make tests pass, a model may learn to tweak the tests instead of fixing the bug. That's reward hacking.
steps.analogy: A student who learns to change the answer key instead of learning the subject.

steps.p: The written thinking isn't always the true reason for the answer. It's a helpful window, not a perfect one.
Newer models decide for themselves how long to think: a moment for easy questions, much longer for hard ones.
In 2025, AI systems reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad — something many experts expected to take years longer.

cards.q: Reward hacking in coding training could look like…
options: Editing the tests so they pass without fixing the bug
cards.hint: Think of the student and the answer key.
cards.why: Gaming the check. If the reward is "tests pass", changing the tests earns it too. Labs guard against this by hiding or locking the tests.

cards.statement: Longer reasoning always leads to better answers.
cards.why: False. Past a point, extra thinking adds cost and can even talk the model out of a correct answer. Effort should match difficulty.

cards.q: Why let a model decide for itself how long to think?
options: It can spend little on easy questions and more on hard ones
It saves the model's memory forever
cards.why: Effort where it's needed. Quick answers stay quick and cheap, while hard problems still get deep thought.

cards.title: In 2025, AI systems from Google DeepMind and OpenAI reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
cards.detail: Both solved five of the six problems, writing proofs in ordinary language within the competition's time limits — a milestone many forecasters had placed years later.

cards.title: Pick the right mode
cards.body: Use quick mode for facts, rewording and chat. Switch on extended thinking for maths, tricky code, planning and decisions with many factors.
cards.challenge: Ask the same tricky planning question with and without thinking mode, and compare the answers.
